title: Rama's name on the tongue
hookLine: a lamp set on the doorstep lights the room and the street at once, and Tulsidas says the tongue is that doorstep
carry: rama's name is a lamp on the tongue

cards: One small clay lamp, and evening coming on. Put it inside, and the house is lit but the path outside is dark. Put it out in the lane, and the house goes black.
Or set it right on the threshold, the step of the open door, where its light falls both ways at once.
Tulsidas, the poet who retold the Ramayana in the language of ordinary people, takes that small household choice and turns it into a teaching about a name: Rama's.

teach.h: SHRI RAM, JAI RAM, JAI JAI RAM.
teach.b: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram. Honor to Rama, victory to Rama, victory, victory to Rama. At a kirtan it rocks back and forth like a boat, and some groups sing it for a long time without changing a word.
Why only the name? Near the start of the Ramcharitmanas, Tulsidas stops before his story begins and spends a long stretch praising Rama's name.

teach.h: A LAMP ON THE TONGUE'S DOORSTEP.
teach.b: In one couplet he gives the lamp picture, in paraphrase: set the jewel-lamp of Rama's name on the threshold of your tongue, if you want light both inside and outside.
The tongue is the doorway between the self and the world, and a name kept there lights both. Then Tulsidas pushes further, and this part can startle.

teach.h: RAMA FREED ONE. THE NAME, MILLIONS.
teach.b: He says the name is, in a way, greater than Rama himself. In the story, Rama freed one woman, Ahalya, the sage's wife who had been turned to stone.

teach.h: GOD IS PRESENT IN THE NAME.
teach.b: The name, Tulsidas says, has turned around the minds of millions. Rama could be in one place at a time. His name can be on every tongue.
This is one of the plainest teachings of Hindu devotion: for devotees, the name of God isn't a label for God. God is present in it.

It's why many Hindus repeat Rama's name quietly through the day, and why, across much of North India, people still greet each other with Ram Ram. The name needs only a tongue to rest on. That's why the song is so plain.

how: At kirtan, Shri Ram jai Ram jai jai Ram is sung back and forth, sometimes for a long stretch without changing a word; some Hindus also repeat Rama's name quietly through the day.

o: a group's songs sung by heart, even just a holy name
a written list of rules for chanting correctly
the poems Tulsidas wrote to tell Rama's story

p: freed by Rama; the name frees millions
praises the name in the Ramcharitmanas

s: Tulsidas says the name only helps those who met Rama in person
he says the name goes on helping anyone who says it, anywhere.
Tulsidas argues that, in a way, the name is greater than Rama himself
Rama helped those he met; the name goes on helping anyone who says it, anywhere.
across much of North India, people greet each other with 'Ram Ram'
the name stays on the tongue all day, even in a hello.

games.q: you have one clay lamp at nightfall. you want light in the house and on the path. where do you put it?
o: on the threshold of the open door.
games.why: on the threshold, its light falls both ways. Tulsidas says to set Rama's name there, on the doorstep of the tongue.

practice: Let the mouth relax, lips just touching, and rest your attention on the tongue lying quiet behind the teeth: that's the doorstep.

If you pray, set Rama's name there, silently, Ram, Ram, and see whether it lights anything, inside or out; if you'd rather not use the name, rest on that doorway anyway and notice what wants to come out of it today.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, Rama's name set like a lamp on the doorstep of the tongue.

orig.note: Rama's name, written in Devanagari. In nama-kirtan, the name alone is the song.

carryVoice: Your line: rama's name is a lamp on the tongue. One name, lighting inside and out. That's day nine hundred eighty-nine.
